title: Konkhunganik
summary: Konkhunganik is the recorded name for the southern part of Fort Pond at Montauk. In the deed language he cites, Fort Pond is described with Quanuntowunk on the north and Konkhunganik on the south.
address_label: Southern Fort Pond, Montauk, New York
map_geometry_source: Approximate/general point for the southern part of Fort Pond at Montauk, based on modern USGS Fort Pond coordinates and Tooker's south-side description; not an exact deed boundary.
why_this_matters: Long before it was known as Fort Pond, Montaukett families utilized the southern shores of Konkhunganik as a recurring seasonal base camp for over a millennium during the Late Woodland Period. Documenting these repeated patterns of habitation highlights the sophisticated ways Indigenous extended families strategically moved across the landscape to harvest Long Island's diverse coastal and inland resources.
translation_content:
Tooker compared Konkhunganik with Algonquian terms for lines, bounds, boundary marks, and marks used to guide travelers. The exact translation remains uncertain, so his reading is best understood as one interpretation rather than a final meaning.

Why Place Names Matter

“Indigenous place names communicate complex cultural, environmental, social, political, spiritual and historical information.”

— First Peoples' Cultural Council, 2022–2023 Funding Recipient List (2023), Place Name Pilot Project description

Names carry language, and language carries community life.
artifacts_content: Among the archaeological artifacts and features found were hearths, shell middens, an oven pit, pipe bowl fragments, and pottery sherds. A total of 475 pottery sherds were recovered resebling the Windsor Brushed and Clearview Stamped design. These are of the local Windsor tradition from eastern Long Island or southern New England, but sometimes Sebonac or Windsor Cordmarked.
land_loss_content: Konkhunganik preserves a Montaukett place name tied to Fort Pond, deed language, and remembered boundaries. Keeping the north-south distinction with Quanuntowunk helps avoid flattening a detailed Indigenous geography into a single modern pond name.
excavation_content: The Payne Site, our current area of investigation, was encountered in 2002 during a Phase I archaeological survey by TRACKER- Archaeology Services, Inc. Subsequent Phase II investigations were completed in 2003 (Cammisa et al 2003A; Cammisa 2002A). [1. Ten Thousand Years of Land Use at Fort Pond: A Portage Haven Phase III Data Recovery Excavations of the Payne Site Montauk, 2008] Tentative evidence for a Paleoindian occupation comes from one broken artifact. A possible mid to late Paleoindian styled unfluted point of white quartzite was recovered. It appears that approximately between 10,000 to 8,000 years ago the property was first utilized by these mega-sized game hunters following large waterways of the bay and/or ocean and likely stopping over at Fort Pond, utilizing the lake as a sheltered haven and portage stop. This may be the first evidence of Paleoindian occupation on Montauk. The Paleo point was recovered in the western portion of the site nearer the water. The point itself is indicative of hunting activity. [1. Ten Thousand Years of Land Use at Fort Pond: A Portage Haven Phase III Data Recovery Excavations of the Payne Site Montauk, 2008 pp 31]
whereintheworld_content: The map placement is a general point for the southern part of Fort Pond at Montauk. It orients the placename and does not claim to mark the exact 1661 deed boundary.
